name: Putamen
func: The outer part of the lentiform nucleus in the basal ganglia. It receives commands from the motor and sensory cortex and helps start, scale and smooth movements, and it stores well-practiced motor habits.

levels.kid:
The **putamen** is a round part deep inside your brain, shaped a bit like a **shell**. In fact, "putamen" means "shell" in Latin!

The putamen helps your body move **smoothly**. When you first learn to tie your shoes, you have to think about every step. After lots of practice, you can do it super fast without thinking. The putamen helps store those practiced moves.

It also helps decide how big or small a movement should be, like a gentle tap or a big kick.

It needs a helper chemical called **dopamine** to work well. Without enough dopamine, moving gets slow and stiff.
levels.hs:
The **putamen** is the large, outer part of the **lentiform (lens-shaped) nucleus**, one of the basal ganglia. The lentiform nucleus has two parts: the putamen on the outside and the paler **globus pallidus** on the inside, separated by a thin sheet of white matter called the **lateral medullary lamina**.

**Location and neighbors** (from outside in): the **insula**, the **extreme capsule**, the **claustrum**, the **external capsule**, then the **putamen**, then the globus pallidus, and then the **internal capsule**. The internal capsule separates the lentiform nucleus from the **caudate nucleus** in front and the **thalamus** behind. At the bottom front, the putamen joins the caudate head at the **nucleus accumbens**, and gray bridges across the internal capsule connect the putamen and caudate, forming the **striatum**.

**What it does:** the putamen is the main motor part of the striatum. It receives signals from the **motor, premotor and somatosensory cortex** and **dopamine** from the **substantia nigra**. It helps:
- Start movements and stop unwanted ones.
- Scale the size and speed of movements.
- Learn motor sequences and turn them into automatic **habits**.

The putamen is the part of the brain most affected by dopamine loss in **Parkinson disease**, which causes slow, stiff movement and tremor.
levels.college:
**Somatotopy:** the putamen maps the body like motor cortex: leg dorsolaterally, face ventromedially, and arm in between. Inputs from premotor areas, supplementary motor area and primary motor and sensory cortex arrive in partly overlapping bands.

**Motor loop:** motor cortex → putamen → **GPi/SNr** → **VL/VA thalamus** → SMA and motor cortex. The putamen sends:
- **Direct pathway** (D1 MSNs) → GPi/SNr. Activating it inhibits GPi, which releases the thalamus and facilitates movement.
- **Indirect pathway** (D2 MSNs) → **GPe** → **subthalamic nucleus** → GPi. Activating it increases GPi output, inhibiting the thalamus and suppressing movement.
- **Hyperdirect pathway**: cortex directly to the subthalamic nucleus (bypassing the striatum) for fast stopping.

**Dopamine** from the **substantia nigra pars compacta** excites D1 MSNs and inhibits D2 MSNs, so overall it **promotes movement**. The **posterior (sensorimotor) putamen** has the densest nigral input and is affected first in Parkinson disease, matching the ventrolateral tier of the nigra, which degenerates first.

**Blood supply:** the **lateral lenticulostriate arteries**, small branches arising at right angles from the M1 segment of the **MCA**, supply most of the putamen, as well as the external globus pallidus and the upper internal capsule. Because they are thin end-arteries exposed to the full pressure of the MCA, they are the classic site of **hypertensive hemorrhage** and **lacunar infarcts**. The anterior part also gets supply from Heubner's artery.

**Other connections:** input from the intralaminar thalamus (centromedian nucleus) and output also to SNr. The **claustrum** next door has widespread cortical connections but its role is still debated.
levels.phd:
**Habit formation:** in rodents, the dorsolateral striatum (putamen equivalent) becomes engaged as actions become habitual. Neural activity forms "**task bracketing**" patterns, bursting at the start and end of a learned action sequence as if packaging it into a single chunk (Graybiel). In human fMRI, activity shifts from the anterior (associative) to the posterior (motor) putamen with extended practice (Tricomi 2009).

**Action vigor:** dopamine affects not just whether an action is chosen but how fast and forcefully it is performed. Animals with low striatal dopamine move more slowly even when they can still move. Optogenetic stimulation of D1 MSNs increases movement, while D2 MSN stimulation suppresses it (Kravitz 2010). However, both pathways are active together during movement, which suggests they cooperate to select one action and suppress competitors, rather than acting as simple on and off switches (Cui 2013).

**Parkinson disease pathophysiology:** symptoms usually appear when roughly half or more of nigral dopamine neurons are lost, and an even larger fraction of putaminal dopamine terminals. Dopamine loss overactivates the indirect pathway and weakens the direct pathway. Both changes raise inhibitory GPi output, suppressing the thalamus. Abnormal **beta-band oscillations** (13–30 Hz) across the basal ganglia correlate with slowness and stiffness and are reduced by dopamine replacement and DBS.

**Dopamine-replacement complications:** over years, the response to levodopa fluctuates and **dyskinesias** may appear. These relate to non-physiological, pulsatile stimulation of dopamine receptors, abnormal plasticity in D1 MSNs and changes in striatal signaling.

**Cell-based and gene therapies:** grafts of dopamine-producing cells into the putamen, now including stem-cell-derived neurons, and gene therapies delivered into the putamen are under clinical trials.
levels.expert:
**Hypertensive putaminal hemorrhage** is the most common site of spontaneous brain hemorrhage, caused by rupture of lenticulostriate arteries weakened by chronic high blood pressure (lipohyalinosis and, as historically described, **Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms**). Patients develop sudden **contralateral hemiplegia** and sensory loss (from internal capsule involvement), gaze deviation **toward the side of the bleed**, and aphasia or neglect depending on the side. CT shows a bright hyperdense clot. Treatment centers on blood pressure control, reversing blood thinners and managing intracranial pressure. Surgery for deep hemorrhages is selective: trials of open surgery (STICH) showed no overall benefit, and minimally invasive evacuation is an evolving option (the ENRICH trial favored it for lobar bleeds).

**Lacunar infarcts:** small deep infarcts of the putamen and internal capsule from occluded lenticulostriate arteries cause **pure motor stroke** and other lacunar syndromes.

**Parkinson disease:** **DaT-SPECT** shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the putamen first, giving a "full stop" or "period" shape instead of the normal "comma." The posterior putamen is affected earliest.

**Multiple system atrophy (MSA-P):** MRI may show **putaminal atrophy** with a "**slit-like**" rim of high T2 signal on the outer edge of the putamen, while the response to levodopa is poor.

**Other conditions:**
- **Wilson disease:** putaminal T2 changes with the "face of the giant panda" sign in the midbrain.
- **Severe hypoxia** can cause bilateral putaminal injury.
- **Huntington disease** (later stages) and **Leigh syndrome** (mitochondrial disease in children).
- **Hemichorea** with high blood glucose in older patients with diabetes shows a bright putamen on CT/T1.

**Surgery:** DBS targets for Parkinson disease (subthalamic nucleus or GPi) lie just next to and below the putamen; gene and cell therapies are injected directly into it using MRI-guided stereotactic techniques.

keyPoints: Outer part of the lentiform nucleus, lateral to the globus pallidus
Lateral neighbors: external capsule, claustrum, extreme capsule, insula
Motor part of the striatum; input from motor and sensory cortex
Dopamine from the substantia nigra; first affected in Parkinson disease
Most common site of hypertensive brain hemorrhage

test.q: The putamen and globus pallidus together form the:
test.explain: The lens-shaped lentiform nucleus has the putamen outside and the globus pallidus inside.

test.q: The small MCA branches supplying the putamen are the lateral ______ arteries.
test.explain: They arise at right angles from M1 and are prone to hypertensive damage.

test.q: Which structure lies immediately lateral to the putamen?
test.explain: From outside in: insula, extreme capsule, claustrum, external capsule, putamen.

test.q: A sudden putaminal hemorrhage typically makes the eyes deviate:
choices: Toward the side of the bleed
Away from the side of the bleed
test.explain: Like other supratentorial lesions, the eyes look toward the lesion.

test.q: DaT-SPECT in Parkinson disease shows reduced uptake first in the posterior ______.
test.explain: The normal comma shape becomes a period shape.

test.q: In Parkinson disease, loss of dopamine in the putamen causes:
choices: Increased GPi inhibitory output and slow movement
test.explain: Dopamine loss favors the indirect pathway and raises GPi output, suppressing the thalamus.
